title: Bouncing Ball Gravity Lab
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: MicroSims
Interactive Simulation
Physics
Kinematics
Predict-Observe-Explain
description: A p5.js MicroSim in which learners predict, then test, how gravity and bounciness sliders change a falling ball's motion and the height of its first bounce.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

educational.topic: Interactive simulation: model plus immediate interaction
learningObjectives: The learner will explain how changing gravity and bounciness changes the motion of a falling ball, by predicting an outcome and then testing it.

accessibility.notes: describe() summary for screen readers; all controls are native HTML buttons, sliders and a checkbox

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.purpose: Run or pause the simulation (starts paused)

controls.label: Drop Again
controls.purpose: Reset the ball to the top and run a new drop

controls.label: Predict first
controls.purpose: Pause after each slider change and ask for a prediction

controls.label: Higher / Lower / Same
controls.purpose: Answer the prediction question (shown only while a prediction is pending)

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter sliders with a prediction gate
keyQuestions: If gravity doubles, does the first bounce get higher, lower or stay the same?
What does the bounciness value represent?
Why does the ball eventually stop bouncing?
commonMisconceptions: Stronger gravity makes the ball bounce lower (it only makes the motion faster)
Bounciness is the fraction of height kept (it is the fraction of speed kept, so height scales with its square)
assessmentOpportunities: Written explanation of why gravity does not change bounce height

equations: at the floor: speed = -speed x bounciness
first bounce peak = bounciness^2 x drop height
assumptions: Motion integrated exactly within each frame
Bouncing stops when the rebound speed is below 0.6 pixels per frame
limitations: Units are pixels and frames, not meters and seconds
